transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-20
Start time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Sara Kim (Quantum Health, Head of ML), Ravi Singh (Platform Eng), Tom Alvarez (Security), Lina Perez (Product)

Summary (auto gen, optional):
Quick discovery focused on integration patterns. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for latency-sensitive healthcare routing. Primary topics: SDK support, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy architecture, rate limits/quotas, observability hooks (tracing/logging), data residency and KMS. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share SDK examples and run a Dedicated benchmark with customer's prompt set.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Maya, AE, and Ethan here is our systems engineer who'll do the technical deep dive.
[00:08] Ethan (Redwood): Hi all. Looking forward to hearing your integration constraints.
[00:12] Sara (Quantum): Hey, Sara here. We're evaluating options for embedding LLM features in our customer triage flows. Latency and PHI handling are the big ones.
[00:20] Ravi (Quantum): Ravi, platform. We own the infra and want to understand networking (VPC, egress), and how a gateway or proxy would sit in front.
[00:27] Tom (Quantum): Tom from security — SOC2, audit logs, KMS questions.
[00:32] Maya: Great. High level, Redwood offers Hosted API, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private/VPC or on-prem deployments. Today we want to focus on where an SDK or LangChain integration fits and what networking looks like.
[00:44] Sara: Our ML team uses LangChain and LlamaIndex extensively. Is there first-class support or examples? Do we need to write a custom adapter?
[00:52] Ethan: Short answer: we have SDKs (Python, Node) and community adapters for LangChain and LlamaIndex. We also have official examples — I can send a repo link. The SDK exposes streaming, function-calling, and chunked embeddings. For LangChain you can use our LLM wrapper; for LlamaIndex there are example ingestion + query snippets.
[01:12] Sara: Awesome. Any gotchas? Tokenization differences, streaming not matching LangChain expectations, etc?
[01:18] Ethan: A few notes — streaming semantics are standard but some LangChain utilities expect particular chunk sizes; we show patterns in the examples to buffer or forward chunks. Also with embeddings, batching is important to hit throughput without hitting rate limits.
[01:32] Ravi: Speaking of rate limits, our internal gateway enforces qps at the edge. What are Redwood rate/quotas? Can we map our gateway limits to Redwood tokens or qps?
[01:43] Maya: Hosted defaults have per-user/token quotas; Dedicated allows configurable rate limits per-route and you can set quotas by API key. For private it's fully controllable. We expose rate-limit headers and a quota API so your gateway can programmatically back off.
[01:57] Tom: For Private, do you support a customer-managed VPC? How does KMS and key ownership work?
[02:04] Ethan: Yes, for Private deployments we offer a private control plane with customer-managed networking. KMS integration with customer keys is supported — you can bring your own key and we won't have access. Audit logs and retention policies can be configured. There are on-prem packages for air-gapped as well.
[02:20] Sara: When you say Dedicated, is data stored by Redwood? We need to limit retention for PHI.
[02:25] Maya: By default Hosted retains short-lived logs for troubleshooting; Dedicated and Private support configurable retention and we can set policies to not persist user data beyond what's necessary. We also have redaction and token filtering options in the pipeline.
[02:39] Ravi: Architecture question — we currently run an internal gateway that does auth and routing to backends. Best pattern is to point that gateway directly to Redwood endpoints, or to run an internal proxy that talks to Redwood?
[02:51] Ethan: Both are valid. Common patterns: 1) Your gateway talks directly to Redwood's public API (Hosted) with mTLS and API keys, 2) For Dedicated/Private, you can put a short-lived internal proxy that handles SSO tokens and rate-limits and then calls Redwood. The proxy can also egress through a VPC peering or private link depending on deployment. We can provide a lightweight gateway example we use with customers.
[03:12] Lina: Any recommended timeout/retry semantics? Our flows are latency-sensitive — sub-300ms for some calls.
[03:18] Ethan: For generation workloads sub-300ms is tough unless models are small and GPU is reserved (Dedicated). For embeddings and rerank, sub-100–200ms is achievable on Dedicated. We recommend streaming for perceived latency. Retry patterns: idempotent retries for embeddings; for stateful generation use token-level resume or fallbacks.
[03:35] Sara: Does Redwood support prefix/KV cache to speed up repeated prompts?
[03:40] Ethan: Yes, our runtime supports prefix caching and KV cache management. For chat-heavy flows where prompts share large context, caching can reduce end-to-end latency and cost. We can suggest cache policies in the Optimize toolkit.
[03:49] Tom: Observability — we need traces tied back to our request IDs and audit logs that include model version, inputs (redacted), and who called it. What's available?
[03:58] Maya: Console has per-request tracing, token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and an API to export traces. You can inject your request-id in X-Request-ID and it shows up in logs. We provide sample dashboards for OpenTelemetry and integrations with Datadog/Prometheus.
[04:15] Ravi: Do you expose streaming metrics at a per-route level? We need to alert on tail latency and error rates.
[04:20] Ethan: Yes — metrics include p50/p95/p99 latency, per-token throughput, error count, and quota usage. You can pull these via the console or a metrics API; we recommend pushing high-resolution traces to your APM for alerting.
[04:33] Sara: For LlamaIndex connectors, when embeddings are computed, do you have a recommended embedding batching size?
[04:40] Ethan: Depends on model and request size. For our standard embedding model we suggest batches of 32–128 depending on token length and latency target. Larger batches are more cost-efficient but increase latency. We'll tune this in the benchmark.
[04:52] Maya: Customer question — how easy is it to pin a model version and roll back if an evaluation shows regressions?
[04:58] Ethan: We have model version pinning per-route, and rollout features (canary/A-B) with automatic fallbacks. The Console shows quality monitors tied to prompt sets so you can detect regressions before full rollouts.
[05:12] Tom: On compliance, does Redwood provide SOC2 Type II and ISO docs? Any FedRAMP talks?
[05:18] Maya: We have SOC2 Type II and are working through ISO 27001. For FedRAMP it's a roadmap item; for highly regulated customers we recommend Private/on-prem deployments. We'll share the compliance pack.
[05:29] Ravi: Networking specifics — for Dedicated, can we use a private link or do you require public egress?
[05:35] Ethan: Dedicated supports private link/VPC peering in major cloud regions. For Private deployments, you fully control network egress. We'll need your network diagram to propose a secure setup.
[05:46] Sara: Any known issues with LangChain's LLMChain streaming when integrating with your streaming API?
[05:52] Ethan: Noted edge cases: LangChain sometimes expects newline-delimited chunks; we provide an adapter that normalizes chunk boundaries. There's also backpressure — the adapter includes a small buffer to smooth streaming.
[06:05] Lina: Cost question — how do you price embeddings vs generation? Is there a per-token + per-embedding unit mix?
[06:11] Maya: Hosted is usage-based; generation is per-token billing, embeddings are per-embedding unit. Dedicated is committed capacity with lower unit costs; we can show a modeled TCO for your expected qps. We'll include a pricing worksheet.
[06:24] Ravi: For our pilot we'd like to test: 1) LangChain Q&A flow using LlamaIndex, 2) embedding index build, 3) streaming generation for triage. Can Redwood run a benchmark with our sample dataset?
[06:36] Ethan: Yes — typical pilot: we stand up Dedicated pilot for a few days, run the workload, measure latency, throughput, and cost. We'll need sample prompts and expected concurrency.
[06:45] Maya: Action items recap later. Quick clarifying question — do you need webhook callbacks for async tasks?
[06:51] Sara: Yes, for long-running indexing jobs we want webhooks and status callbacks.
[06:56] Ethan: We have async job APIs with webhook callbacks and retry semantics; we'll include sample code.
[07:03] Tom: Security follow-up — can audit logs be exported to our SIEM?
[07:07] Maya: Yes, we support log export to S3 or direct streaming to your SIEM and have an API for audit exports.
[07:15] Ravi: If we put a proxy in front, will token-level observability be lost?
[07:19] Ethan: Not if you forward the original headers (Request-ID, user identifier) and include the request metadata in the proxy call. We can show header mappings.
[07:28] Lina: Do you have roadmap items around LangChain native hooks or more SDKs?
[07:33] Maya: We're planning first-class LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors in the next quarter, plus additional SDK features like built-in retrievers in the SDK.
[07:41] Sara: One operational concern — can we enforce per-tenant quotas inside our workspace to limit users experimenting?
[07:48] Ethan: Yes, per-route and per-api-key quotas are supported. You can map tenants to API keys and enforce hard quotas.
[07:56] Maya: Ok, let's recap next steps and owners.
[08:00] Maya: Ethan will run a Dedicated benchmark with your prompt set; we'll need the sample prompts and concurrency. Ethan, owner?
[08:07] Ethan: Yep — I'll run it. Targeting results by Aug 27.
[08:10] Maya: I'll send the SDK quickstart, LangChain/LlamaIndex snippets, and the compliance pack.
[08:15] Sara: Tom will share any specific audit/export requirements and the network diagram.
[08:19] Tom: Will do — sending by Aug 24.
[08:22] Maya: We'll also share a draft pilot and Dedicated pricing.
[08:25] Ravi: How long is the pilot typically?
[08:27] Maya: Often 3–7 days of dedicated runs for benching, then a 30-day pilot for integrations depending on scope. We'll tailor it.
[08:36] Lina: Any blockers from our side to start the benchmark?
[08:39] Ethan: Need sample prompts, expected qps/concurrency, and any special data redaction rules. Also credentials for test environment.
[08:48] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[08:51] Sara: Thanks — excited to see the benchmark.
[52:00] Meeting end.
